source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.1, printed pages 7-8: atomic radius and its trends (Figure 1.4).

blocks.text: The atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom: half the distance between two identical atoms bonded together. It can vary with the type of bond (covalent, metallic or van der Waals) or the state of the atom; the radius in a covalent bond differs from that in an ionic bond. It is measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms.

blocks.alt: Atoms drawn as spheres sized by their radius, in old groups 1 to 8 across and periods 1 to 6 down: H and He; Li to Ne; Na to Ar; K, Ca and Ga to Kr; Rb, Sr and In to Xe; Cs, Ba and Tl to Rn. An arrow along the top reads 'atomic size decreases' (left to right) and an arrow down the left side reads 'atomic size increases'.
blocks.caption: Fig 1.4: Variation in atomic radius across periods and down the groups (original drawing after the textbook's Fig 1.4).

blocks.text: The factors affecting the atomic radius are the atomic number, the effective nuclear charge and the shielding effect of the inner electrons. Generally the atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right, because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer. Conversely it increases down a group, because additional electron shells are added and more shielding makes the atom larger even though the nuclear charge also rises, which is outweighed.
